newsitem.title: ITALY: INSTANT VIEW-Italy April CPI seen at 1.8 pct y/y.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Italy April CPI seen at 1.8 pct y/y.

text.p: Following are economists' reactions to the preliminary 0.3 month on month rise in Italian April CPI and the 1.8 percent year on year rate estimated after six cities' inflation data released on Monday.
Analysts in a Reuters survey had forecast on average a monthly rate of 0.2 percent and yearly rate of 1.8 percent. March CPI was 0.1 percent and 2.2 percent respectively.

Alessandro Fugnoli, strategist at Caboto brokers, said: "The market is expecting a rate cut this week. The Bank of Italy has the room to cut but it will also have the room in May and June. The window of opportunity will last more than a month.
Asked how big he expected the cut to be, he said, "Probably 50 basis points, the Bank from now on will be very careful."
Naples, Venice, Turin, Milan, Trieste and Bari announced their preliminary April data on Monday. The other five sample cities will issue their figures at 1530 GMT on Tuesday.
The final official figure will be issued on May 6.

Marco Pianelli at Nomura London told Reuters Financial Television, "This is clearly good news. There is a chance that the month by month rise will be 0.1 percent which will take the year by year figure to 1.7.

"I think the Bank is clearly going to ease but there is no urgency to do it today. They want to make sure that the market is at ease with a rate cut and they may wait till the final data is out on May 6," he said.
Lucia Trevisan of Caboto agreed that Tuesday's cities' data could be better than expected, giving an overall year-on-year rate of 1.7 percent.
"Today's figures are a conflicting," said Alfredo Granata of Banca di Roma, noting a month on month rise of 0.3 percent in Milan and a monthly 0.6 fall in Trieste.

"I imagine the cities due on Tuesday, like Florence and Bologna, will come in along the lines of Milan so confirming an annual 1.8 percent rate. But there's still the possibility of seeing 0.1 percent monthly and 1.7 percent yearly," he said.
Caboto's Trevisan said although the data looked good it did not automatically mean the central bank would move immediately to cut rates.
"A cut isn't 100 percent discounted given the global situation. Early elections in France could in fact weaken the lira via the French franc," she said.
